utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Good morning. Please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning. Case number IT-95-9-T, the Prosecutor versus Blagoje Simic, Miroslav Tadic, and Simo Zaric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. The next counsel, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to all present in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Mitrovic. My name is Novak Lukic, I defend Mr. Miroslav Tadic before this Tribunal. I do not have many questions for you; just very few. We shall use these questions to clarify a number of issues that arose in your answers to the Trial Chamber yesterday. First of all, I would like to ask you a number of questions related to the membership of my client, Mr. Tadic, in the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the witness please be shown document D59/3.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you please have a look, and we'll place the document on the ELMO. You can look at it while it's actually on the ELMO. This document was not shown to you yesterday. Very well. Mr. Mitrovic, my first question: Are you familiar with the fact that Miroslav Tadic was appointed commander of the civilian protection staff in Samac?

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can we then agree that it is by virtue of his position as the commander of the civilian protection staff that he became a member of the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't provide an accurate answer to this question. I mean, whether it was an automatic thing that on the basis of his position there he became a member of the Crisis Staff. I can't answer your question. I am not familiar with that. I do not know whether that was the basis for his becoming a member of the Crisis Staff too.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just tell me what you know. I am not insisting on you providing answers that you are not certain of, but we can, can't we, agree that throughout the first days and months during the shelling and war destruction, the role of the civilian protection staff was essential for the functioning of everyday life in Samac?

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you could say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Have you ever seen this decision before? Because you didn't mention yesterday that you typed up a number of decisions. Do you know anything about this specific decision? I want to know about the preamble.

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I'm reading through it and the preamble, and I can't recall this specific decision. At least, I can't remember actually typing this decision or participating in making this decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We'll no longer be needing this document. Now can the witness please be shown document P82.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yesterday, Mr. Mitrovic, you testified about this document which will again now be placed before you. It's a decision on the commission for the exchanges. I will ask you several questions about that document and about your testimony yesterday. Judge Lindholm asked you whether you had any direct information concerning the provision contained in Article 2 of this decision, and you said you didn't know anything about that. Now, can you please have a look again -- look through this document, and Article 2 specifically. My apologies, this is not the same document. My mistake. I'm sorry. Just a minute, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] P83. Yes. A decision on the commission for the exchanges. I think it's dated the 2nd of October.

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Article 2, more specifically, states that "The commission will function in cooperation and with the approval of the security organs of the 2nd Posavina Brigade and the bodies of the Public Security Station. My question is: Do you agree with my client's position that in order to obtain approval for the exchange of detained persons you needed to go to the SUP or, rather, to the security organs of the 2nd Posavina Brigade? Do you have any direct knowledge of that?

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as these affairs were concerned and how they were carried out by Mr. Tadic, the methodology -- or rather, the methods he used to do his work are not known to me. However, this document clearly shows which organs and institutions took part in carrying out these tasks, the tasks stated here, the exchange of detained and other persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I was asking you about your direct knowledge. Anything else will obviously be interpreted by the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Another question about your direct knowledge of certain events. If you don't have any, please just say no. Did you know that civilians who wanted to be exchanged reported to the local Red Cross of their own free will? Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no direct knowledge, as I said, of how these activities were taking place, of who was in charge of carrying out these tasks. I do know, however, that for a certain period of time Mr. Tadic was in charge of these activities. How he went about these tasks and activities, I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And do you know whether Mr. Mastic, who was hereby appointed president or chairman of the commission also worked on these exchanges, even before the decision was adopted?

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know why Tadic was merely appointed a member here if he had worked on the exchanges before and another person was actually appointed chairman of the commission?

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You were, as you said yesterday, Mr. Mitrovic, if memory serves me, the Secretary of the Municipal Assembly, and stayed in that position until 1997; isn't that what you said?

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know, in the period between the time in January 1993, when the assembly was reconvened, and after that, did Miroslav Tadic hold any official position in the municipal organs from that time onwards, while you were there, aside from his work on the exchanges?

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since 1993, when the assembly started meeting again as a full-fledged assembly, I was not aware of Mr. Tadic being a member of any -- of the assembly's commissions boards or working bodies. He was not even a deputy there.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Mr. Maslic, do you know whether he was the head of the centre for social welfare or did he hold any official positions in the assembly?

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I only met Mr. Maslic for the first time during that period of time. I later found out that he had been an employee of the centre for social welfare in Bosanski Samac. Whether he was head of that institution or not, I'm really not sure. But over the following period he was involved in the work of the executive board of the Municipal Assembly of Samac. He had been appointed by the assembly. I think he was in charge of social affairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We'll move on and talk about something you already testified about yesterday. Judge Williams asked you about the War Presidency, and you mentioned, I think on page 19 of yesterday's transcript, that as far as you could remember a decision had been adopted at the republic level. I'm talking about Republika Srpska, on setting up War Presidencies.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the witness please be shown document P72. It is a decision on the establishment of War Presidencies throughout the municipalities during the imminent threat of war or state of emergency, signed by the president of the presidency of Republika Srpska, Dr. Radovan Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Please have a look, because you were not shown this document yesterday. I want to know specifically about Article 2 and Article 5, but please take your time and you can read through the whole decision. You can actually take the document and have a look.

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mitrovic, is this the decision you referred to yesterday when you told us about your information concerning the setting up of War Presidencies? Is this the same decision you were talking about yesterday?

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I learned about this decision when we received our copy of the Official Gazette, and I know that it was with a certain delay, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Please go on.

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: However, I made a suggestion to Mr. Simic at that time that maybe it would be a good idea to reconvene the assembly. However, he said that the conditions were not in place for the assembly to be reconvened and that this would happen at a later date, once conditions were created. If you ask me about this decision specifically, and in relation to the War Presidency of Samac Municipality, I think it was on the basis of this decision that the Crisis Staff was renamed and became War Presidency.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That's exactly my interpretation of Article 2, paragraph 5, where it says that "Crisis Staffs cease to work once War Presidencies are established." I suppose you will agree with me on this. You also said yesterday, and you mentioned now, that sometimes you received your copies of the Official Gazette with delay. But tell me, please, if you agree with me: This decision was published on the 8th of June, 1992, and Article 5 clearly states that within 15 days it will be set up, and we do know that the decision on the War Presidency in Samac was adopted in mid-July. Is this connected to the fact that you spoke about, that you received your copies of the Official Gazette with a certain delay?

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think that's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Very well. Let us now please look at Article 2, which contains the envisaged composition of the War Presidency and its members. You will agree that Miroslav Tadic was not a republican commissioner in the Samac municipality?

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I suppose we can also agree - and this is an agreed fact in this case - that he was not the president of the municipal assembly or the deputy. He was not the president of the executive board or his deputy.

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You will also agree that he was not a deputy and not a member, was he?

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I was listening to your testimony yesterday, and you said you couldn't say with any degree of certainty who the members of the Crisis Staff were. It is an agreed fact that Mr. Tadic was - and we are not disputing this - but can you tell us whether Miroslav Tadic was or was not a member of the War Presidency?

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe the members of the Crisis Staff remained in place and continued to be members of the War Presidency. They continued their work. As I said yesterday, as far as I know, those were Dr. Simic, Mr. Tadic, Mr. Simeun Simic, Mr. Savo Popovic. That's as much as I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You said yesterday that you were not told when you were drafting the decision whether new members were to be appointed or not.

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Formally speaking, you did not receive a decision naming the members of the War Presidency.

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will no longer be needing this document for the time being. Can the witness please be shown document P82 now.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This is a letter to the Holy Archidiaconal Synod. You testified about that letter yesterday and you explained how Stevan Todorovic literally dictated this letter to you and told you expressly what the letter was to say. I will not ask you about the content of this document, but Judge Williams asked you yesterday whether you remembered talking to Mr. Tadic about Patriarch Pavle's concerns in relation to the arrest of a priest, and you said there was no reason for him to talk to you about that. Now, my question is - I will try to remind you of the following, my client's position: Do you recall prior to the drafting of this letter whether Miroslav Tadic visited Patriarch Pavle to talk to him about other matters, and did he convey any information to you or to Stevan Todorovic in your presence? Can you recall anything like that?

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues] ... the document is on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, it's a public document. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: This is a public document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I will tell you what the position of my client is. He claims that he did see Patriarch Pavle in Belgrade in relation also to the Serbs detained in Odzak, that they talked about the detained priest, and then upon his return from Belgrade he conveyed this information on the premises of the Crisis Staff to Stevan Todorovic, who was there, and you were there too. He claims he conveyed this information there. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do remember that. When this happened, I can't remember whether it was Mr. Tadic, but that's possible. There was a person there who was supposed, in relation to this event and this letter, to go immediately to Belgrade to see the Patriarch. Whether it was Mr. Tadic or not, I really can't remember right now, but I know that there was a person who was there, but the situation was very difficult and I told you about the circumstances at that time. I can't remember whether it was Mr. Tadic specifically.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Tell me, can you remember at all whether you actually held in your hands a letter sent by the Synod to the Municipality? This letter, does it state the source from which His Excellency found out about the priest who had been arrested? Does the letter say anything about that?

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that there was a document that had arrived from the Patriarch in Belgrade in relation to this case, and this document was the subject of a heated debate in the office between Dr. Simic and Todorovic. I can't remember what the document actually said, the whole content of the document. I know there was this debate, a quarrel even.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Mitrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions for this witness, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Pisarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Mitrovic. As we know, because you testified about your position as Secretary of the Municipal Assembly and Secretary of the Crisis Staff of Samac Municipality, I will ask you a number of questions about your method of work, or rather, how the whole thing functioned. As you said, you were in charge of the technical drafting of these decisions and such. Tell us, please: Were any kind of records kept of decisions adopted by the Crisis Staff? I did notice that all the decisions and everything decided by the Crisis Staff had a number, a record number, which is -- which every decision has and bears. Can you please tell us something about that.

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. At the Crisis Staff there was a book, a book in which enactments of the Crisis Staff were being recorded. This book was also used to record enactments that I put together. I don't know whether all the enactments of the Crisis Staff and the War Presidency were actually recorded in that same book. I do not know because I was not there the whole time, especially in the period, as I said before, of May, June, and July 1992. Yesterday I looked at a number of documents that I couldn't recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the witness please be shown document P79 ter. Very well. Thank you. That's fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mitrovic, this is an announcement, as you can see, and in the upper left corner it says "Crisis Staff, number 01-2/92." Correction, 01-10/92. Did you type this announcement actually, or rather, did you add the bits that are in handwriting? Is this your handwriting?

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Can we agree that according to this information, this number where it says "01," that this was actually the first, the very first decision ever adopted by the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not know that this was the very first decision adopted by the Crisis Staff. I heard about this announcement because I believe it was published in the media and it was published several times, several days in a row. Now, whether it was the first document ever adopted by the Crisis Staff, no, I really can't say.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: But you are a person dealing with records, assigning file numbers to documents. So please tell us: I've noticed this other number, number 10, where it says "01-10," I've noticed on most decisions of the Crisis Staff this number 10. Was that some kind of a mark or a code indicating that this was a decision by the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think that was any special kind of mark or code. I was not the one assigning numbers to these documents really. The records were kept at reception, which in May, June, and July 1992 was occupied by a lady whose name I can't remember. I think her last name was Tesanovic. She was keeping the records of the Crisis Staff in May, June, and July. Or rather, I think it was Mr. Savo Popovic who was there keeping the records in that office.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: You were therefore telling us that that number 10 is not a special code or a special number indicating the body that will adopt decision.

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not know if that number means anything special. I don't know if this is an indication which tell us that this is a body of the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness please be shown a document bearing number P112.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: You have seen this decision already. It is a decision regarding the creation of the executive board. It is a decision dated 30th May 1992, a decision about the creation of the executive board. You can see that on the top we can see "Crisis Staff, Municipal Assembly of Bosanski Samac." Then we see a number, "139-10/92," dated 30th May 1992.

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: So could you please tell us, what does this number 139 mean?

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This number is supposed to be the number that's recorded in the book of records. It is the number of the enactment entered in the book for the enactments of the Crisis Staff. If I remember correctly, it was in chronological order that these numbers were inscribed. So all the documents, not only the official enactments, but all the other documents were also inscribed and put there, all the technical documents that have no special bearing with regards to the work of the Crisis Staff, for instance. If I'm not mistaken, there was also an order for food, orders for food, for fuel, were also put into this book and were also given a number.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes. But what is this -10? What does that mean?

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know, you want me to tell you about the number 10.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Does this mean that this was everything that was stemming from the Crisis Staff as a body that existed at the time? Does that mean that all the orders, all the decisions, or whatever, was stemming from the Crisis Staff and that was sent to other bodies? Does that mean that this is what it represents? Does it mean that all these -- everything that was stemming from the Crisis Staff bore that number 10?

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm telling you again, I am not the one who was recording all of these things, but it is possible because this number 10 appears in all the documents of the Crisis Staff or the War Presidency, so at the very beginning I was not the one who was recording documents. I can just suppose that this number, since it appears up until the very end, it probably means that this is a number that means that, that it is -- it means that it's a document stemming from the Crisis Staff or the War Presidency.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Then I will not ask you any more questions regarding this. But all those enactments were recorded, as you say, and when the War Presidency was created you told us that the enactments were also recorded in the same fashion. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now I would like to witness to be shown the document P83 ter. Could you please move the document in such a way that we can see the number. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Very well. At the very bottom of this document we can see a number 213-10 1992 or rather, 213-10/92, dated 7 of October, 1992. And we can see that it is a decision stemming from the War Presidency.

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: And this number 213 is the number of this document; is that correct? And this number 10 would be a number indicating that this document stems from the Crisis Staff; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is so.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. We do not need this document any more. Could the witness please be shown the document D55/1 ter.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mitrovic, you saw this document yesterday, if I'm not mistaken.

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: I would only like to ask you one thing about this document: I believe that yesterday you wanted to add something which you didn't have the time. You see that under number 12 we see a handwritten note, Topcagic Fadil, we can see that it says "Member of the Crisis Staff," and we see some numbers. Do you see this inscription?

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Were you the one who added this with your own hand?

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was a little surprised yesterday, I must say. I was surprised when I saw the content of this document, and I must say that I am not sure if this is a -- an authentic document, even with regards to my signature. On the left-hand side we see the signature of Mr. Mirko Lukic. If I recall correctly, his signature -- yesterday I said that these -- that this data with regards to the positions held by these people are completely inaccurate, and I must say that some interventions were made here, later on with regards to the dates, and some additions were made, such as this particular name was added, and on the right-hand side we see some amounts - and I do not agree with them - I actually have some doubts as to the veracity and the authenticity of this document, and I already stated - and I'm sorry to interrupt you - but I would like to say and restate once again that I was never a member of the Crisis Staff. This document is not ...

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Excuse me. I will interrupt you. Please tell us, did you add yourself with free hand the name of Topcagic Fadil on the top of this document?

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, absolutely no.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Can you tell us to the best of my knowledge and to the best of your -- to the best of your knowledge, can you tell us if Mr. Topcagic Fadil was a member of the Crisis Staff in the month of May 1992, or rather, did you ever see him attending any of the meetings of the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: With regard to the sessions that were held in May, June, and July, sessions that I attended, I was present while these sessions were convened, or I was there. I did not see Mr. Topcagic Fadil. I did not see him come to the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We will not need this document any more.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: You stated yesterday that during the session of the Municipal Assembly of the Municipality of Pelagicevo which took place on the 16th of December, 1992 in the village of Pisari you told us that the commission was formed, the commission that was to present to the assembly during People's Assembly the adoption of all the decisions of the Crisis Staff for ratification. Was that done? Did this commission actually do this in such a fashion?

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this commission, if I'm not mistaken, was convened, and if I'm not mistaken, all the enactments from the War Presidency and from the Crisis Staff were submitted to this commission. Everything that was available was handed down to this commission. This commission looked at these documents, and at a later session proposed to the assembly the decisions and the enactments, and it was up to them to verify all this.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: So the result of that commission, the result of the work of that commission, wasn't the agenda of an assembly -- of a session?

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Are those all the documents and all the decisions that were published in the Official Gazettes later on when you were able to publish all these documents, when the technical -- when you were technically able to do so?

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This commission was -- proposed these enactments and the assembly was to verify them, and if I'm not mistaken those enactments were enumerated and it went to the assembly in such a way. So the assembly only had to verify certain enactments. And if I'm not mistaken, I think it's general enactments. Those were general enactments.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: So the commission gave a proposal to the municipal assembly, and the municipal assembly had to verify these enactments and decisions of the Crisis Staff and of the War Presidency and the assembly was to verify these documents.

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: It was to ratify. Correction.

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Do you know if there were any decisions that this commission did not propose to the assembly, decisions that were adopted by the Crisis Staff and by the War Presidency?

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This commission had within their possession what was available for myself and what was available from the records, from the file of the enactments of the Crisis Staff and the War Presidency, and then therefore that commission enumerated all these decisions and they're the ones who proposed what was going to go for ratification. So whether all the enactments were sent for ratification, I don't know. If some of the documents were not sent, I cannot give you a clear answer. I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Can we agree that the documents that were not proposed by the commission for the assembly to ratify as decisions stemming from the Crisis Staff, in fact those documents were never ratified on behalf of the Municipal Assembly of Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Pisarevic, you cannot ask that question. This witness has said he doesn't know whether any decisions were not ratified. Now you are giving evidence and asking the witness to agree with you. That is not correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I withdraw this question.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Who was in charge of keeping these records, with regards to the work of the Crisis Staff and the War Presidency?

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know if somebody was in charge of keeping the records. These records were at the Crisis Staff, and there's -- there was a book of records where all these decisions were placed and it was at the reception desk, if you will, if I may say so that way, and this book of records was not kept by a particular person. The protocol and the records were not particularly protected. So when I would come there during the time when I worked there, in May, June, and July, it was not under lock and key. The archives were not sealed off, they were not protected in a special way.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You told us about May, June, and July, but I'm interested in 1993, 1994. What happened then, from 1992 to 1994? Who was keeping these records?

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The records of the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Who was in charge of keeping the records?

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1993 or in 1994, if I'm not mistaken, those records were handed down to Dr. Simic, if I am not mistaken, all the records of the Crisis Staff and the War Presidency, all this -- all these records, those files, were handed to the president, Dr. Simic, and he kept them in his office. So after 1993 and later, they were in his possession.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. The cross-examination by the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Could I just -- before I start, could I just correct something I said yesterday in relation to some documents. I said yesterday that Mr. Lukic -- Mirko Lukic submitted them to us, and I thought -- understood that Mr. Pisarevic -- it may have been through Mr. Pisarevic. We have checked those. It was my confusion. It was in fact through Mr. Mirko Lukic, not Mr. Pisarevic at all, and I withdraw any suggestion that he had any hand in it.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Mr. Mitrovic, I'm going to ask you some questions based upon your evidence of the last day or so for the Prosecution. As a lawyer, you understand my role here as the Prosecutor, don't you?

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Now, sir, when you asked -- you answered some questions a moment ago about the detention of a priest and representations made by the Patriarch in Belgrade for his release. I just want to make sure that we have completely got the transaction clear for the -- for the Trial Chamber and for the record, and can I suggest -- or can you clarify that it was this: Firstly, a letter arrived from the Patriarch to the Crisis Staff, number one?

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Secondly, Todorovic saw the letter, there was a discussion or an argument between him and Simic, he dictated the letter to you - that's Todorovic - and Simic told you to send the letter off? That's the second thing in the series of the transaction.

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's exactly how it happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Thank you. And the third was that someone then - you can't remember who - then after you had sent the letter then went to Belgrade to make personal representations to the Patriarch?

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I am absolutely certain that there was a person who immediately left for Belgrade. I don't know if it was the next day, but I think so. And this person had the task to go see the Patriarch in Belgrade and that person was to explain and was to find an appropriate answer to this problem. I'm just trying to go back in time, to rewind the film of my memory, if you will. I don't remember if it was Mr. Cedo Simic or Mr. Tadic. I'm not quite sure who it was, but I know that somebody did go, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Thank you. I was interested in the sequence, one, two, three. Now, in 1990 -- I withdraw that. Your evidence is that you have a law degree and I think you were born in 1964. When did you leave school, Mr. Mitrovic?

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I graduated from the Faculty of Law in the month of October or early November 1991. It is a fact that I was not very knowledgeable in the works -- or in that kind of work, the work that I started doing, in the public domain.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What did you do between November 1991 and April 1992 when you had this job of Secretary of the Crisis Staff or Municipal Assembly?

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As of the 1st of December, 1991, up until the second half of April, I worked in a company. It was an agricultural company. They were -- they gave me a job as a lawyer of that company, so it was my first job ever and I was a trainee, actually, at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Was that a state-run agricultural company or a private one?

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a -- it was an agricultural association, and I don't know if in France or in Holland you have such a thing, in Western Europe. I don't know how to explain. I can try to give you the status of that company. It's a bit specific.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: If I could ask you some direct questions on it. The directorship of the company, who appointed the directors or the managers of the company? Was it the farmers themselves or was it the municipality or some other person or institution?

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understand your question. This company was not appointed by a -- by the government. It was the peasants, if you will, or the farmers, people who were working within this cooperative, and they were the ones who appointed the head of the company.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Where was this job located?

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Obudovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: When you were at university, did you have any political affiliations or were you involved in political organisations on campus or in your home town or anywhere else?

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not at the time. When I was at university, I had other activities. I was a member of -- I was a scout.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What about your family and your wife? Were the members of your family or does your wife have political affiliations at that time? That's 1991/1992.

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. None of the members of my family in 1991 were involved in any political activities, not at the time, and they're not involved even today.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Were you mobilised in 1991 or 1992?

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe it was at the end of 1991. I couldn't really tell you the month. But I did receive a call. It was the federal army at the time. And I was called for an exercise of the reserve formation, and I think I spent seven days at that exercise and that was it.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Were you a member of any of the detachments of the 17th Tactical Group of the JNA's 17th Corps, that is, the 1st, 2nd, 3rd, or 4th Detachment of the 17th Tactical Corps -- Tactical Group, I'm sorry?

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I was called, and then I had this exercise which lasted seven days as a member of the reserve unit. Now, I don't know if they were linked with the tactical group. However, I do know that afterwards I came back to work in the company in question.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Are you related to any of the three accused over there, either by marriage or by family?

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: How long have you known Dr. Simic for?

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was at that time that I met Dr. Simic, at the beginning of these activities in 1992 and during the period of time that followed in 1993 and 1994, as the president of the municipality of course he was also my superior, so to speak. So it was during that period of time that I was able to know him better.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Did you develop a friendship with Dr. Simic over that time?

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can give you the following answer to that question: We cooperated very well over certain periods of time, but our opinions also differed on certain issues. These disagreements culminated in 1996 when we had opposite positions on certain issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Were they work-related issues? I don't want to go into this, but were they - yes or no - work-related issues or other things?

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it had to do with the indictment issued by this Tribunal. It was my belief that it was necessary to act as it had been ordered in the Dayton Peace Accords, that we should act accordingly, that a different president should be appointed given the fact that the agreement specifically provided for the persons indicted by the Office of the Prosecutor of this Tribunal, that they could not be appointed to any public office, and we had differences of opinion of this particular issue. I cannot say that Dr. Simic personally took part in this, but I will take the liberty to say that after that certain SDS circles in Samac retaliated, with respect to myself personally and my family, concerning my employment, and my wife, as late as the year 2000, was forced to leave, was actually sacked.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What about Mr. Tadic, the defendant -- the accused Mr. Tadic? You know Mr. Tadic, don't you?

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: All right. Is -- how long have you known Mr. Tadic for?

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was also during that period of time that I met Mr. Tadic. It was either in late April or early May 1992. I had not known him prior to that. Our contacts actually boiled down to just a couple of encounters, when he came to visit the town hall or to attend the session of the assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And what about Mr. Zaric? You obviously know Mr. Zaric as well. How long have you known Mr. Zaric for?

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know him as well as I know Mr. Tadic. I personally saw Mr. Zaric and I met him on -- I cannot recall the precise date, but I know that it was on the occasion of his being proposed by Dr. Simic to an office within the Ministry of the Interior of Republika Srpska. After that I saw Mr. Zaric just a couple of times. But as I said, those were just superficial meetings or encounters. I didn't have any specific contacts with him concerning the actual work.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: This office with -- the office he was proposed -- sorry, the office which Dr. Simic proposed him within the Ministry of the Interior of the Republika Srpska, was that the position of chief of National Security Service within the Samac municipality in the state of emergency? Is that the one you're referring to, or is it something else? And that is P81, for the record.

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, that is the event in question.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: All right. If I could just go back to your -- I withdraw that. The -- I think your evidence yesterday, or the effect was, that you received an assignment or a work obligation to work as the Secretary of the Samac Municipality at the time of the -- or publication of the "imminent threat of war" in Samac. Have I got that right? Is that the effect of your evidence yesterday?

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was on the 15th of April that the imminent threat of war was proclaimed on the territory of the then-Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and I was appointed Secretary of the Municipal Assembly on the 28th of March, but after this imminent threat of war was proclaimed my position was activated, that is, after the 15th of April I was tasked by the Ministry of Defence to perform this work until the situation is resolved. The imminent threat of war lasted until I think either the month of May or June 1996. It was until that period of time that the imminent threat of war was proclaimed -- lasted.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I'm just trying to clarify something from your evidence, and that is this: You'll agree that in October 1990 there were elections in Bosnia and a democratically elected local assembly, that is, the Municipal Assembly of Bosanski Samac was elected? You'd agree with that, wouldn't you?

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And of course this Samac Municipality, of course - you'll have to agree - was a Serb-only institution, based upon the constitution and its composition?

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you please clarify. What do you mean by "a Serb-only institution"?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The Serbian Municipality of Samac was a Serb institution comprised of Serb -- sorry, SDS deputies and deputies of Serb ethnicity. You looked at the -- I think Their Honours showed you the constitution yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see. Yes, I see what you mean now.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I understand you question.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Would you agree with that basic proposition that it was a Serb institution, formed by the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, on the basis of the decision issued by the Assembly of the Serbian People in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And based on that, it was a parallel government to the existing elected government. That's of March 1992. There's evidence before the Tribunal that that was the case, and I'm just asking you to agree with that basic proposition. It was a parallel government or institution existing at the same time as the elected one?

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These institutions were publicly proclaimed in Sarajevo in 1991 and 1992. I think that three Official Gazettes of the Serbian people were published to that effect in Sarajevo. It was a public thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: By the constitutional court --

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Please, what I'm just asking you is to accept that there was an elected municipal assembly and there was this parallel Serbian one, both existing at the same time in March 1992. You'd agree with that, wouldn't you?

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. As far as I know, the deputies of the Serbian assembly were the same ones that had been elected in 1990. I was not there when this assembly was constituted in February, but I know that that was the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And the purpose of this parallel or Serbian assembly, according to the proclamations or the Official Gazettes of the Serbian people, was to form a government in the municipality then called Bosanski Samac, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can say that this parallel government, as you call it, was established on a condition in case it becomes necessary to defend vital interests of Serbian people in the area, if my understanding of the issue is correct. The constitution of Bosnia-Herzegovina was violated.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The purpose was to form a government in a municipality if necessary, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Your evidence is that the Republika Srpska's Ministry of Defence - I think it was the Ministry of Defence. Correct me if I'm wrong - appointed you to the position of Secretary of the Assembly - that's the Serbian -- of the Serb assembly - before the 15th of April, 1992, that is, as of the 28th of March, 1992. Is that your evidence?

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But the Ministry of Defence merely confirmed or verified the situation as it was at the time and my position, my appointment.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You're saying the Secretary of -- or the Ministry of Defence verified or ratified the Serbian -- the Serbian Assembly of Samac appointing you as the secretary on the 28th of March and you received some official notification of that as a work obligation around the 15th of April; is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In my military booklet which contains information on my assignments or work obligation during the time of war or the imminent threat of war, the Ministry entered the information on my assignment within municipal authorities. That was specifically stated in my military booklet.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And you received that before you reported for duty as Secretary of the Crisis Staff; is that so?

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not immediately, because normally you keep the military booklet at home, but I had to bring it to Samac on a later date, and I think it was Mr. Bogdanovic who entered this particular information on my assignment in this military booklet.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What I'm trying to get to, Mr. Mitrovic, is your appointment as the Secretary of the Samac Serbian Municipality. At the time you said you were working as a lawyer, your first job out of law school for an agricultural cooperative. This job of Secretary of the Assembly of the Serbian Municipality of Samac, it wasn't a job that was advertised, was it?

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, of course not.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: As far as you know, there were no other applicants for the position?

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The -- go on. You were going to say something.

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in such conditions, in such circumstances, especially with respect to such positions and in the situation when it was the Ministry of Defence who assigned people to their particular military or work obligations, defence regulations apply under these circumstances, and it was that ministry that was in charge of appointing or assigning people to various jobs, without any prior vacancy announcement.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Mr. Mitrovic, you weren't the only lawyer in the municipality of Bosanski Samac at the time, were you?

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was not.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Mr. Mirko Lukic, for example, has legal qualifications.

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: There were other lawyers of Serb ethnicity working for the Municipality, weren't there?

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot remember the names, but I'm sure that there were such lawyers working there. I mean, in the municipality at that time. But I really don't know who they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The position was a -- a very responsible one. You'd agree with that, wouldn't you, being a Secretary of the Municipal Assembly? It's a very responsible position?

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yesterday I tried to respond to Her Honour Judge Williams, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Please just concentrate on the question. I'm asking you whether -- I'm asking you to agree or disagree with --

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues] ... so the answer is yes?

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No audible response]

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Mitrovic, your evidence was that you were six months out of law school -- or less than six months out of law school, doing your first job working in an agricultural company. How did you become known to those at the Serbian -- or the Serb Municipality executive who appointed you to that position on the 28th of March, 1992?

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time the assembly that met on the 28th of March was held in the town where I worked for this particular company. The venue was in the vicinity of the company I was working at the time, and the people who knew me -- I mean, it was probably the people who knew me who proposed me as a lawyer to this position, without any particular reasons or conditions.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Mr. Mitrovic, you were working -- you had a job at the time. You must have been surprised when you were told that you were going to -- into this new, very responsible position for someone less than six months out of law school, in their second job. You must have been surprised about that.

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I must admit that I was, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And you must have asked how it came to be that I, Mitar Mitrovic, lawyer for the agricultural co-op, have now been catapulted into the Secretary of the new Municipality? You must have asked that.

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you're referring to that period of time and to the town of Samac when it was established on the 15th of April -- or are you asking me about the 28th of March?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: When you found out that you had this new job by order of the Ministry of Defence to be the Secretary of the Serbian Municipality, you must have -- you must have asked how it came to be. Who did you ask?

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was my work obligation and my war obligation that I had to comply with, regardless of my personal opinion on the whole issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Let me just go back. You were elected on 28th of March, 1992 -- or appointed to the position. You know that. What I'm asking you is: Just based upon normal human experience, you must have been extremely surprised to find yourself elevated from Secretary of the Co-op -- sorry, lawyer of the co-op, junior lawyer of the co-op, to Secretary of the Municipality. In relation to your appointment at the meeting on the 28th of March, who did you ask about your appointment and what were you told?

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course it was something that I did not expect, so it did come as a surprise for me, but I assume that at the time there was no specific -- there was not much choice amongst other lawyers --

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What I'm asking you is: You said you were surprised. You must have asked someone, "How did I, Mitar Mitrovic come to be appointed or elected for this position?" Who did you ask? You must have asked someone. Who did you ask and what did they tell you about what happened on the 28th of March.

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I spoke with Mr. Ilija Ristic, who was the president of the Serbian Assembly at the time. I also discussed it with the vice-presidents of this assembly, Mr. Blagoje Simic, and Mr. Dusan Tanasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What did Mr. Dusan Tanasic, Mr. Ilija Ristic, and Dr. Blagoje Simic say to you about the circumstances of your appointment and why you were appointed? But firstly, tell us when the discussion was and then move to the second part.

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I discussed it with the -- these individuals in Obudovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: When?

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 28th of March.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What did they say to you?

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They explained to me what the situation was and what the reasons were for the establishment of this assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Just please tell us --

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: -- what they said to you. Just not explain the circumstances. As best as you can. I know it's a long time ago. What did Dr. Simic, Mr. Tanasic, and Mr. Ristic say to you? They said, "Mitar ...." Da da da da da. Just tell us what they said to you.

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I'm trying to explain to you what it was that they told me. They explained to me what the situation was and they mentioned the reasons for this and they told me that the situation was urgent and that the municipal organs -- the assembly organs had to be established as soon as possible and that I should accept as a temporary solution this appointment until such a time, until the entire situation in Bosnia and Herzegovina becomes clearer.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And did they tell you that you would be the Secretary of the Crisis Staff once it was established? That is, that your duties of the municipal -- Secretary of the Assembly would also be Secretary of the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, absolutely not. There was no mention whatsoever of such possibilities or plans.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What did Dr. Simic say to you on the 28th of March in Obudovac about the circumstances or the situation? As best as you can, what did he say to you was the circumstances of the situation?

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he told me, together with these other people that I mentioned, Ristic and Tanasic - there were other people who were attending the session as well - he told me what the political situation was, he explained to me the decision of the People's Assembly of the Serbian Republic. He said that it was our duty to establish Serbian assemblies on the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina until appropriate political solution to the situation, which was very difficult at the time in Bosnia and Herzegovina, was found. The problems had been caused by this decision adopted by the Assembly of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina concerning the holding of a referendum on independence of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina without the consent of one of the three constituent peoples, that is, the Serbian people in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What did he say was the urgency of the situation?

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He only said that it was necessary for this to be put on paper, that these bodies should be established until the overall situation caused by the referendum on independence is resolved in Bosnia-Herzegovina. As to what would happen and how it would happen, I really -- I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: In relation to that discussion with Dr. Simic on the 28th of March in Obudovac and your appointment as the Secretary of the Assembly, was that before or after you were appointed on the day? Did they ask you before whether you were willing to accept the position or did they tell you about the fact that you had been appointed to it afterwards?

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On that day, the 28th of March, I was simply called up during that session or during the break of that session in Obudovac. There must have been a discussion regarding the appointments and the work of the assembly, and at one point they invited me to come over from my company and they simply asked me whether I would agree to this temporary employment, and they also explained to me what I -- what I had just -- have just told you about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: We will take our break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, the Prosecution is continuing.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Mr. Mitrovic, I just want to ask you to assist us as much as possible by -- can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I want you to assist us as much as possible in terms of time and the clarity of your evidence by giving direct answers to the questions I ask. Do you understand?

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: My earlier question was: How did you find out about your appointment? And ten minutes later we still hadn't found out. So I'm just going to try and summarise what you just told us. The question I asked you could have been answered very directly. I just want to pose a direct question to you and I just want you to answer it directly, please. Can you help us with that?

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. So can I please summarise what happened about you finding out about your appointment, or the fact that you had been propose as a Secretary of the Municipal Assembly of Samac, the Serbian one? Firstly, you were at work; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Someone telephoned you and said, "Come to the assembly meeting"?

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not telephoned. People came.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Someone sent people over from the assembly, the assembly session, and I went there. I did not attend at the very beginning of that session.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You came in to the assembly session some way after -- sometime after it had commenced; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: At the time that you entered the assembly hall, was the meeting in progress?

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: When you got there, were you greeted by Dr. Simic and Mr. Tanasic and Mr. Ristic or did they speak to you afterwards during a break?

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They spoke to me during the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Thank you. All right. We'll move on. At the time they -- when you arrived at the -- sorry, when they spoke to you, had you -- had -- your name had been put forward for the position of secretary but you had not been elected or appointed yet; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And during the break, Simic, Tanasic, and Ristic took you aside and asked you if you would accept the appointment of secretary; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And that is how you found -- and you said, "Yes, I will accept the position of Secretary of the Serbian Municipality"?

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And you stayed for the balance of the meeting, the remainder of the assembly session, or you left to go back to work? Do you remember?

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't stay for the remainder of the assembly session, I believe, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You were informed -- well, were you there when the vote was taken as to your appointment as secretary?

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: So you left the assembly meeting knowing that you had been appointed or elected as Secretary of the Serbian Municipality?

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I left the meeting just before it drew to a close. There was one last item left on the agenda when I left, appointments to the executive board.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Well, why couldn't you just have told me that when I asked you directly about an hour ago and Her Honour Judge Williams when she asked you how you came to be appointed yesterday? Why couldn't you have just said that quite directly?

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- that was not the way I understood the question. Now I'm giving you the specific answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. I'll move on. Now, you said you were living Obudovac during May, June, and July 1992. Was that your evidence yesterday?

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Were you staying in Samac or -- sorry, Bosanski Samac at any time during that period, in a house or flat in Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: During that period, I would be called to the Crisis Staff or the War Presidency. I spent the night at the Crisis Staff several times. During that period, as I said yesterday, I was in Obudovac on Mr. Simic's instructions at a staff building, staff for the protection and evacuation of persons, and that was also where I slept in Obudovac, in that building.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: This morning you gave evidence about the declaration of the state of emergency in Bosanski Samac, that is, P79. And you said you heard about it in the media. You said it was published. Was it -- did you hear it over the radio, Mr. Mitrovic?

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That declaration, the first time I saw that declaration was when I arrived in Samac, and I think it had been forwarded to Mr. Antic, I believe, a journalist, whose task was to publish it over the radio, or maybe he had already announced it on the radio. I saw this declaration or announcement at the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The Crisis Staff would no doubt have been interested to know whether it had been broadcast on the radio. Did Mr. Antic report to the Crisis Staff or did you see any documents to the effect that it had in fact been published on the radio -- over the radio?

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't see any documents to the effect that it had already been published over the radio, but I do know that later the announcement was actually published or broadcast over the radio.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: When you say "later," how later?

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The next day, or the second next day. Mr. Antic came to the Crisis Staff, and he would come there to see Mr. Simic, I assume - I assume - I assume why.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What about its publication in the media? Was it published in a magazine, a newspaper, or nailed on boards around the town? Where did you see it published?

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether there were public announcements on boards around the town. I saw the announcement declaration at the Crisis Staff, and I learned from Mr. Antic. He told me that it had been broadcast on the radio, which Mr. Simic also told me, that it was on the radio. Mr. Antic, I believe, had received the task to -- to have this broadcast on the radio.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What about publication in the paper media, newspapers, magazines? Did you see it in any newspaper or magazine or hear about its publication?

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: During that period of time, I don't think any paper media were being published. I don't remember this being published or publicly announced in any of the written media. If I'm not mistaken, in late April and in May no official newspapers were being published. There was an official newspaper called -- the official newspaper in Samac. I can't remember this at the moment. But I think Mr. Pisarevic and Simic probably know, but the newspaper stopped being published in late April, because I assume they were not able to keep on publishing.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: So the primary means of the Crisis Staff or the assembly communicating its decisions [Realtime transcript read in error "decision"] to the population was over the radio; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I did not talk to Mr. Antic specifically about the publishing of this announcement, but I heard this from Mr. Simic in our conversations and at the Crisis Staff while I was there, that this had been broadcast on the radio.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: There's an error in the transcript. The question I actually asked you was its decisions, not that particular decision. Was the Crisis Staff's primary means of communicating its decisions in the period when you worked there over the radio?

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I believe I understand your question. I do remember that at the beginning of the period there was a publication, a newspaper, rather, that was called the Koridor, but they began publishing this paper much later as a written media. They were not the official mouth piece of the Crisis Staff or of the War Presidency. This newspaper was published by a company which had in the meantime been activated. I believe the manager of that company was Mr. Simeun Simic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Who was a member of the Crisis Staff or attended Crisis Staff meetings.

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The Crisis Staff communicated to Mr. Simeun Simic the decisions it wanted published or things it wanted published, proclamations, et cetera, in Koridor, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember the exact date when the Koridor newspaper began to be published, but I do know that Mr. Simeun Simic was in charge of information and public communications with the Crisis Staff for a while.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Can we just go back to my question. My question was: The Crisis Staff communicated to Mr. Simeun Simic -- or Simeun Simic the decisions it wanted published or things it wanted published, proclamations, et cetera, in Koridor, didn't it? Regardless of the date, the Crisis Staff or War Presidency told him what they wanted published.

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not have any direct personal knowledge as to what Simeun Simic's task was, in terms of publishing.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Yesterday you were shown a -- I withdraw that. We'll just go back to this in a moment. The Koridor magazine, was it discussed during Crisis Staff meetings? Copies were put around the table and Crisis Staff members looked at it and discussed its content? Did that occur?

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you talking about the Koridor?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The Koridor magazine, not the Posavina Corridor.

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This magazine was published and publicly distributed in the municipal area.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's --

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Are you having difficulty with the question? Well, the question was: Was it discussed at the Crisis Staff? Please answer that one and not another one.

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no knowledge of that, in terms of the Crisis Staff specifically discussing any of the media, or that magazine specifically.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: All right. We'll move on, then. Yesterday you were shown a document. It's P113, which was the authorisation of Stevan Todorovic to attend the Bosanski -- sorry, the Serbian -- the Assembly of the Serbian Republic meeting to be held on the 25th of July, 1992. You remember being shown that document and you remember the evidence you gave on that yesterday?

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You said Dr. Simic asked you -- or dictated to you or gave you -- or told you what to put in the authorisation.

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Where was Dr. Simic when he gave you the instructions to sign the -- to type and sign this document?

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Simic, I can't remember his specific location, but I know that he went to Belgrade for medical treatment.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: He must have done it -- you didn't go to Belgrade to type out this letter, did you?

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: So it occurred in Bosanski Samac, didn't it, his instructions to you?

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I can't remember the circumstances, but I know that Dr. Simic instructed me to give the letter to Mr. Todorovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You didn't go to see him in hospital and he gave you the instructions, did you?

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did see him in hospital once, to see Dr. Simic. I can't remember whether it was the same date, related to this enactment.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And when you saw Dr. Simic in hospital, was it in your capacity as Secretary of the Crisis Staff and he in his capacity as President of the Crisis Staff and you went to see him to discuss Crisis Staff or War Presidency business?

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I went to Belgrade because my family was staying there, so I used the opportunity to also visit Dr. Simic while there.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Now, how long was Dr. Simic out of action for in hospital in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, specifically the amount of time he spent there, I can't remember, but Dr. Simic should know the precise period of time he spent there. I really can't give you a specific time frame now, the period of time that he spent there.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: All right. It's just the document says that the above name - that's Todorovic - is to represent and act for the municipality as a member of the War Presidency -- sorry, as member of the War Presidency due to the justified absence of the president of the War Presidency, who is in hospital for being -- being treated for a gunshot wound. That's dated the 25th of July, 1992. The document seems to indicate that he was in hospital at the time you signed the authorisation. I'm just interested in how Dr. Simic communicated the instructions. Was it by telephone?

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Todorovic came and said that he had urgent orders to be signed and that he did not have the authority to sign them because he could not sign his own orders but that he had received oral permission from Mr. Simic and oral instructions from Mr. Simic, and he said that this approval had to be issued to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And as a result of that, you checked with Dr. Simic. That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not have an opportunity to check with him right away, but I had no reason to doubt the allegations of Mr. Todorovic. Mr. Blagoje Simic, upon his return from Belgrade, didn't tell me anything about this document, nothing along the lines of not having given his approval.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I just want to clarify something in relation to your evidence yesterday, Mr. Mitrovic. Page 41 of the transcript, His Honour Judge Lindholm asked you some questions about the document, and the questions were:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: Do you recognise this document? Answer: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: It is signed by yourself answer. Answer: Yes. Yes. I had the authority to do that by Dr. Simic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: Wasn't there a deputy president within the Crisis Staff? Answer: I don't know whether a deputy was appointed or who that was, but I do remember this document and I remember that Dr. Simic ordered me to sign it. I believe that he at the time was absent or supposed to be somewhere. In any case, he ordered me to forward this urgently to Mr. Todorovic. Now, that's what you said yesterday when Judge Lindholm asked you some questions. Can you please explain how that fits with what you just told us.

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What this means is that Mr. Todorovic had received authorisation from Mr. Simic. I had no reason to doubt Mr. Todorovic's statement. Mr. Todorovic was a very authoritarian person. It would have been impossible for me to try to discuss with him the authenticity of Mr. Blagoje Simic's instructions.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Sir, when you said yesterday, "I remember that Dr. Simic ordered me to sign it. I believe that he at the time was absent or was supposed to be somewhere. In any case he ordered me to forward this urgently to Mr. Todorovic," what you meant was Mr. Todorovic -- hang on -- Mr. Todorovic ordered -- asked me to sign it and told me that Simic had said it was okay and on that basis I believe that Simic had ordered me to sign it? Is that how you could explain the difference between what you said yesterday and what you said today, or is there some other way of explaining it?

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think there is no difference between these explanations, as far as the case related to the detainee when Mr. Todorovic was also involved. It's the case we discussed yesterday.
