So there was no doubt. Mr. Blagoje Simic never told me later that he had not granted his approval, which for me meant that the approval had been granted.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Of course it was approval for Mr. Todorovic to attend a -- an assembly meeting of the Serbian Republic. That's basically the Bosnian Serb parliament, as the representative of the Crisis Staff. Dr. Simic was the normal representative of the Crisis Staff for the Bosnian Serb Assembly, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And Dr. Simic attended meetings of the Bosnian Serb Assembly when he could get away from his duties as the president of the Crisis Staff or War Presidency in Bosanski Samac, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not know how many meetings of the parliament or the assembly Mr. Blagoje Simic attended, but he probably did attend those meetings in certain periods of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You say you don't know how many, but you know that he attended some. That's what you're saying, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe he was in possession of a decision by the Crisis Staff or, rather, authorisation to attend and to represent Samac Municipality at the parliament and in the bodies of Republika Srpska. He did not go to any great lengths to give me explanations or any information regarding these matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The attendance of a representative from the Bosanski Samac Municipality was important for the municipality in terms of its relationship with the Bosnian Serb Assembly, wasn't it, because it enabled the Municipality to know directly what was happening at the national level and speak to people, speak to officials there and communicate your views or make representations?

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assume so, if I understood your question. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: That's why it was important for someone from Samac to attend as many -- to attend as regularly as possible the meetings of the Bosnian Serb parliament. You'd agree with that, wouldn't you?

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And I believe that representatives of all the municipalities attended meetings of the parliament.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What do you recall Mr. Simic reporting back to the Crisis Staff or War Presidency about his attending those sessions? What do you remember about reports he made or what other members of the Crisis Staff said or War Presidency said in relation to his attendances at the Bosnian Serb Assembly?

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I cannot really tell you with precision this. I don't know if Mr. Blagoje Simic explained anything at the Crisis Staff meetings or the War Presidency meetings, if he explained the situation that prevailed at the parliament of the Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Do you remember -- do you remember other members of the Crisis Staff or War Presidency discussing with him in advance, before he went to the meetings, telling him what sort of things they wanted him to raise with officials in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I don't have that kind of personal knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What about Mr. Todorovic? The document authorises his attendance at that Bosnian Serb Assembly meeting on the 25th of July. What did Mr. Todorovic, if anything, say to the War Presidency upon his return about -- about his experience of attending the Bosnian Serb Assembly for the first time?

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If Mr. Todorovic talked about the information and if he gave a report to Mr. Blagoje Simic regarding the meeting, I don't know because I was not present, and Mr. Blagoje Simic is probably the one who could explain to you what his relationship was with Mr. Todorovic, as to whether Mr. Todorovic gave him certain information.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Mr. Mitrovic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: You have exhausted your one hour. One hour, which you were allowed to examine this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: You started at 9.50.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The Prosecution has a number of things it wishes to put to the witness. Your Honours may have noticed when I simply asked the witness how he was appointed to the assembly, it took almost 15 minutes to get a direct answer. There are a number of topics that I wish to go into very briefly but I have not been able to because a lot of the answers haven't been direct to fairly simple question. The Prosecution has a number of -- about five separate discrete topics I wish to ask him about, but I cannot do so if I can't get direct answers to direct questions, which does not in the time permit the Prosecution to put its case properly to this witness. And there are several things I wish to explore, which in my submission are important for the determination of the case. So I'd ask Your Honours if you could perhaps give me -- I can probably do it in half an hour, if Your Honours give me that time, which in the context of the case and the importance of this witness, in my submission, isn't -- wouldn't unnecessarily prolong proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: The Trial Chamber is of the view that all the parties were given one hour and the Prosecution was informed about that. They know -- they had the subpoena. They knew the areas that this witness was going to cover. And it's the duty of the Trial Chamber to control the proceedings so that everybody is fairly treated, as far as the time is concerned. And as far as the Trial Chamber is concerned, it doesn't appear that there is any more evidence that this witness can cover which has not been covered by other witnesses. So the Trial Chamber will give you 15 minutes to complete.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You gave some evidence earlier about Mr. Maslic. I want to clarify something from your evidence earlier about Mr. Maslic and the Red Cross, that you said he was involved in the work of the executive board. I want you as briefly and directly as possible to tell us in bullet-point form if possible what were -- what he did in terms of his involvement in the work of the executive board.

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Maslic was appointed as a member of the executive board in charge of social duties. In other words, he was in charge of education, culture, health care system, and other social activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I want to ask you about the Red Cross. He was involved in the Red Cross. The municipality, was it providing money -- that is, the Samac Municipality, was it providing funds to the local Red Cross?

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not know. I do not know if the Red Cross had any dealings with the executive board, but they cooperated.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: They cooperated. What was the extent of the cooperation -- what can you tell us about the cooperation between the executive board and the Red Cross?

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not know this. I don't have any direct knowledge, because I did not take part in this, but the Red Cross, as well as other similar organisations and institutions, are always linked to the competent organ of the executive board in charge of social activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Did Mr. Maslic or Mr. Vasovic or any members -- representatives of the Red Cross attend the Crisis Staff or War Presidency meetings to report back or receive instructions or information while you were there?

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not have this type of information. I do not recall. Perhaps I wasn't present during those meetings where the activities of the Red Cross were discussed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The short answer is you don't know. Okay. Thank you. We'll move on?

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, I want to ask you about -- it's been asked several times that in May, June, and July, who did your duties when you did not attend Crisis Staff or War Presidency meetings? Who was the person who sat in for you, the acting secretary on the meetings you did not attend?

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Thank you. The Crisis Staff had several stamps, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not know how many stamps it bore. There was a stamp at the Crisis Staff; I know for that one.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The Crisis Staff, it issued -- you had a stamp, Dr. Simic had a stamp. That's correct, isn't it? You both had stamps for your work, you as secretary, and he as president of the Crisis Staff, of the War Presidency?

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know how many stamps there were available, but I know that stamps were used. Dr. Blagoje Simic was in charge of the stamps. All the signatures that would appear on the stamps, or at least I can speak for myself, they were all made according to the instructions given by Mr. Blagoje Simic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And he controlled the issue of stamps, did he?

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I'm just trying to find out -- and you had access to one for your stamping of the documents which you had to stamp and the documents you signed in your own personal capacity -- or sorry, your own official capacity as Secretary of the Crisis Staff or the Assembly?

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the stamp was at the office of the Crisis Staff, and as far as I know, the stamp was not under any particular protection. It was not kept in a certain special area.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic and Their Honours asked you about a document D55/1, which is the payroll of the War Presidency, which has your name on it as a member. You said you had some doubts about its authenticity. Now, this document was put into evidence by Dr. Simic. What causes you to doubt its authenticity?

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For instance, correcting a document, adding a name of a person, the change of a date, for instance, even when it comes to my own signature I'm not sure that this is my own signature, and I especially started having some doubts when I saw that I was considered to be a member of the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The Crisis Staff issued authorisations to several people to travel abroad, that is, to -- to another country, that is, Serbia, to approach people and organisations for assistance, didn't it? And they were Slavoljub Nikolic, Vidoje Nikolic and yourself?

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was shown some documents yesterday and those documents are unknown to me, the documents that I saw yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What about your own authorisation? The Crisis Staff or the War Presidency authorised you, didn't they, as their representative to travel to Yugoslavia to obtain -- to travel outside the country if necessary to obtain assistance for the people of Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not know. I do not recall. I do know that I went to Belgrade and that I asked for assistance. If I recall correctly, it was an association for Serbs [As interpreted] from Bosnia and Herzegovina, and I talked to a man. What was his name now? Let me see. I think it was Gajic, if I'm not mistaken. That was his last name. And this man represented this association, if I recall correctly.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: When did you go to Belgrade --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Pantelic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I do apologise to my learned friend and to the Trial Chamber. It's line -- it's page 51, line 16, just for the sake of clarity. Witness said that that was association of Serbs from Bosnia and Hercegovina, not for Serbs. I mean, just a correction to be clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. That will be corrected.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Mr. Mitrovic, the month and year, as best as you can, when you went to Belgrade? Nothing else, please.

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't remember. Was it in 1993 or another year? I really cannot remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Did you travel outside Bosanski Samac on behalf of the Municipality of the Crisis Staff seeking assistance any other time in 1992 and 1993?

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't recall travelling. I really don't recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What were you doing in May, June, and July in Obudovac? That's in 1992.

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since at the time the Crisis Staff was established and it was operational and I was the secretary of the actual municipal assembly and Dr. Blagoje Simic told me at the time that my presence was not indispensable at all times during the meetings of the Crisis Staff, so he sent me to Obudovac, where I come from, to give my assistance to a unit for evacuation and it was a humanitarian organisation. Obudovac was in a very difficult situation at the time. A lot of refugees were coming from the surrounding areas and they were all coming to Obudovac, so that unit in charge of the evacuation and accommodation, and I can tell you that Novak Tenasic was the head of that organisation, that organisation was in charge of giving assistance and accommodation to that population, but they were also in charge of the local population as well. And I can recall that even for the local population we had organised some works, such as building, in Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Mr. Mitrovic, there's evidence before this Trial Chamber that a meeting -- this is for the Court's benefit at page 9082 -- a meeting in Crkvina on the night of the 16th and 17th of April, 1992 at about 1.00 a.m. at which Mr. Jovanovic, Dr. Simic, Mr. Bogdanovic, possibly Mr. Simic, and -- Simeun Simic, and you were present. What can you tell the Trial Chamber about the meeting at about 1.00 a.m. on the night of the 16th, the 17th of 1992 in Crkvina?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Before the witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Pantelic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: -- can answer, Your Honour -- I do apologise to my learned friend, just for the sake of -- to be fair with the witness. Meaning of "evidence" in common law jurisdiction and also between -- before this Trial Chamber -- I mean, this Tribunal is rather different than the meaning in our legal system. So in fairness to the witness, maybe the term "evidence" should be replaced with, let's say, "statement of witnesses" or, you know, some kind of -- I don't know, "documents, if any," so it should be more specific to this witness. Otherwise, me might be confused that this "evidence," under the marks, notation, might be for him indisputable evidence, which is of course in dispute in this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: But your intervention doesn't mean anything, because the Prosecution has simply said there's evidence that there was a meeting and the witness can answer to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. But I'm speaking in terms of the language, B/C/S translation. The word "evidence" in our language is more strict in this particular -- because, for example, it is not evidence in our legal system, statement of witness before the Trial Chamber. It is not evidence. The evidence is only a fact which is determined by the Trial Chamber after the proceedings. So in that sense I kindly ask my learned friend to say that, for example, there was a statement of various persons or witnesses before this Trial Chamber that this meeting occurred in Crkvina, something like that. That was the basis for my intervention, Your Honour. Otherwise, the witness can be confused, because the meaning -- the term "evidence" in our language is rather different than in English language and in common law jurisdiction. That's the basis, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may. Your Honour, I would just like to add something. I believe that the Prosecutor by asking questions in this fashion is asking questions about something that the Trial Chamber has already decided on. I don't know if the Prosecutor would like to confront this witness with the testimony of another witness. I don't know what is on that page. But I believe that the Trial Chamber has already decided that such a procedure would not be allowed. I believe, and I concur with my colleague, Mr. Pantelic, that one could ask questions in a different way, because the Trial Chamber has already decided and stated that it is not allowed in this court proceeding to proceed this way, that is, to confront the witness with the testimony of another witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I'm happy to rephrase the question, as Mr. Pantelic suggests, to make it clearer for the witness. But I'm not confronting the witness. I'm following the Trial Chamber's clear instructions, which are not to put the direct testimony and say X said such and such but to say there is evidence before this Trial Chamber of X, what do you say to this? That's simply what I'm doing. But I'm quite happy to rephrase the question to evidence is stated by someone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Re. You can proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Mr. Mitrovic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: You can rephrase your question. It's been quite a lot of intervention.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: It was four minutes ago, and it's disappeared. I had to find what it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Mr. Mitrovic, my question was: A witness has given evidence -- or a witness has made a statement before this Trial Chamber of a meeting occurring in Crkvina on the night of the 16th and 17th of April, 1992 at about 1.00 a.m. In which the participants were Mr. Jovanovic, Dr. Simic, Mr. Bogdanovic, yourself, and possibly Mr. Simeun Simic. What can you tell the Trial Chamber about that meeting?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Objection. [Interpretation] Objection, Your Honour. The Prosecutor only changed the word. He said "witness" but did not change the word "evidence." So why doesn't he ask the following question: Mr. Mitrovic, were you present at the meeting at such and such a date? But one cannot confront the witness with a statement of another witness, and you members of the Trial Chamber have already ruled on this. But I have the feeling that my learned friend is trying to confuse the witness and put forward to him that another person is stating something different. This is the basis of my objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues] ... the Trial Chamber there was a meeting, he was there --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What can he say about it? That's all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Re, can we get out of this problem. Just ask him whether he attended such a meeting and what transpired, who was present. All right?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I thought "what can you tell us about the meeting" wrapped all things up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Re, can you just follow instructions of the Trial Chamber and go ahead?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Of course, Your Honour. Of course I will.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: This meeting about which a statement has been made to this Trial Chamber, were you present at that meeting?

utterances.speaker: MITAR MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I can't take it any further. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Mitrovic. I think we have finished with your evidence. You may leave the courtroom. Did you want anything, Mr. Pantelic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I thought maybe -- do I have a right for a redirect?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: No, no, no, no. This witness was called by the Trial Chamber, and you were given your time to ask questions. And these instructions were given long before the witness came. Can the witness be led out of the courtroom, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: The Trial Chamber has been informed that there is no other witness today, unfortunately, because the other witnesses we are given to understand are only coming in today, for Thursday and Friday. The Trial Chamber has been informed, Mr. Pantelic, that the Victims and Witnesses Unit haven't got any particulars of the witness in place -- you're calling in place of Mr. Krajisnik, so they are -- they cannot start making arrangements for his travel, and this would delay the witness coming.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I will explain, Your Honour. Mr. -- Dr. Stanko Pivasevic will be able to arrange his passport today or at latest tomorrow, since we got our Orthodox -- Orthodox Easter these days, and it was not possible for him on a short notice to apply for -- for a passport. Dr. Pivasevic is one of the -- the only person, I could say, in the medical centre of Samac. And before Easter he was on permanent duty, around the clock, so he was not able physically even to apply and go to -- to the police authorities, which is 70 kilometres from -- from Samac. I believe today or tomorrow he will -- because he is -- he is a deputy, he is a member, MP, he's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Look, Mr. Pantelic, this isn't the first time we are having anybody from that area coming here as a witness, and the Victims and Witnesses Unit always assist witnesses obtaining these travel documents as soon as they are told about the particulars of the witness, which you haven't done. So it's no use telling the Trial Chamber because you haven't done your work properly, and this is not the first time that -- you are always delaying giving the particulars of your witnesses to the to Victims and Witnesses Unit for them to start working on these travel arrangements.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I do apologise deeply for this inconvenience, if there is something for the Defence, I take all responsibility. But --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. But it doesn't pay to keep delaying the calling of your witnesses when in fact you -- you are representing the first accused and your witnesses should have been completed by now.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, just for your information, just a week ago the instruction of Dutch Ministry of Foreign Affairs came to our attention through Victims and Witnesses Unit saying that specifically passports for Bosnia-Herzegovina should be applied.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: That -- that is old news. We have been informed about that sometime back, and that was the problem with the previous time, which was explained to the Trial Chamber and the Victims and Witnesses Unit are well aware of that problem, so there is no reason to waste time on this.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I'll do my best by the end of this week to arrange everything. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. And he's replacing Dr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: So he will stick to the evidence that Dr. Krajisnik was supposed to give.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: And we have a list here -- it doesn't include Mr. Marko Tubakovic, Mr. Pisarevic. He's also supposed to come, and the Trial Chamber the last time did say that he ought to come as soon as possible so that he can complete his evidence before Mr. Simo Zaric.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, absolutely. Your Honour, we have taken all the necessary measures. Mr. Tubakovic will arrive to The Hague on Saturday and he will testify on Monday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you. Very well. There being no other business, the Trial Chamber will rise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 1st day of May, 2003, at 9.00 a.m. 22 23 24 25
